group.passage: Kenya is making impressive strides in the global avocado market, rapidly climbing the ranks of top exporters. While Mexico and Peru still lead, Kenya has already surpassed South Africa to become Africa’s largest avocado exporter and now ranks third worldwide. Last year, there was an impressive 24% increase in Kenya’s avocado exports, the highest growth rate among major producers. Several factors have contributed to Kenya’s success. The country’s highlands, at 1,500-2,100 meters above sea level, provide ideal growing conditions. Heavy annual rainfall (about 1,000 millimeters in some areas) means irrigation is only needed during the four-month dry season. Most Kenyan farms use less than 100 liters of water to grow a kilogram of avocados, significantly below the global average. The consistent equatorial sunlight also benefits the fruit, allowing it to “grow by day and go to sleep at night,” as one industry executive describes it. Export timing advantage in the global market as well as low labor costs play pivotal roles, too. Kenya’s avocados ripen before many competitors’, and some fortunate orchards even produce two harvests annually due to multiple rainy seasons. Small-scale farmers have quickly adopted avocado cultivation, with trees yielding good crops within just a few years. In terms of labor costs, Kenya’s minimum monthly wage for farm workers is approximately $57, compared to $280 in Peru, though larger producers often pay above $90. This cost efficiency translates to retail prices — rural Kenyan markets sell ripe avocados for about eight American cents, while British supermarkets charge $1-2 per fruit. Even when global demand continues to grow, with Americans consuming 44% of worldwide imports and Europeans showing increasing appetite — German consumption rose 10% last year, and Polish consumption jumped 24%, challenges remain, however. Last year, agricultural authorities temporarily banned exports after some farmers, especially smaller ones lacking proper storage technology, shipped immature fruit with poor texture. On the other hand, international shipping presents additional difficulties. The Gaza conflict has closed Red Sea routes, forcing longer journeys around South Africa that increase costs and spoilage risks. Despite these challenges, Kenya is currently endeavoring to enhance its maritime logistics infrastructure and shipping technological capabilities, which will certainly ensure high-quality standards to preserve its reputation. It is evident that Kenya’s avocado industry will flourish alongside other green initiatives in this renewable energy-leading country.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following statements about Kenya’s avocado industry is true?

options.A: Kenya is second to none when it comes to avocado exports.
options.B: Kenya has lower average labor costs compared to its competitors.
options.C: Kenya ships its avocados mainly to the United States and European countries.
options.D: Kenya relies only on its natural advantages to play a role in the global avocado market.

questions.stem: What does the industry executive mean with the statement “grow by day and go to sleep at night”?

options.A: He compares his produce to pets that exhaust their energy in the daytime and rest at night.
options.B: He highlights how a consistent climate routine contributes to the quality of Kenyan avocados.
options.C: He displays a sense of pride in how farmers profit from Kenyan agricultural development.
options.D: He expresses his sympathy for how hardworking Kenyan avocado farmers have been.

refers_to.text: grow by day and go to sleep at night

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, what does the word “ones” refer to?
How does the author feel about the impact of challenges described in paragraph 4 on Kenya’s avocado industry?
